title: #9 Erik Sprinchorn on Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)

reader_summary.headline: Welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye.
reader_summary.overview: Welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye. I'm your host, Eddie Palngen, and with me in the studio is my colleague, Nicholas Savos. And today comes another episode where we talk with a fund manager about a book of their choice.

key_points.text: So, Nicholas, who is our guest this time?
key_points.evidence_quote: So, Nicholas, who is our guest this time?

key_points.text: We have the great pleasure to introduce Eric Sprincon, who is a portfolio manager at Tin Fonder in Stockholm.
key_points.evidence_quote: We have the great pleasure to introduce Eric Sprincon, who is a portfolio manager at Tin Fonder in Stockholm.

key_points.text: Eric has been a portfolio manager for over 25 years at various firms, and launched Tin Fonder in 2019, together with Carl Armfeld.
key_points.evidence_quote: Eric has been a portfolio manager for over 25 years at various firms, and launched Tin Fonder in 2019, together with Carl Armfeld.

key_points.text: Together, they had a very successful spell at Swedenk-Rober, co-managing their technology fund.
key_points.evidence_quote: Together, they had a very successful spell at Swedenk-Rober, co-managing their technology fund.

thesis: The guest argues that humans naturally use self-justification and dissonance reduction to avoid admitting mistakes, a tendency that becomes more dangerous and prevalent as one's public status increases. He suggests that overcoming this trap requires the difficult but necessary act of letting go of ego and truly owning up to one's errors.
